paper.title: Does early childbearing matter? New approach using Danish register data
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference are given. …

registers.role: linkage / sample frame (family links and demographic variables; mothers connected to children through family links and personal identification numbers)
treatment/comparison-group construction (all pregnancies categorized as completed or aborted, distinguishing miscarriages from induced abortions) and health controls
outcomes: yearly earnings and adult earnings
outcome (education length) and controls (parental education level)
outcome: hourly wage rate (Fig. 4 Panel B) and summary statistics

linkages: The parents in the sample are connected with their children through family links and personal identification numbers (FABE up to 1986, BEF thereafter)
Sisters are defined as women with a shared mother; Table A7 restricts the samples to sisters who also share a father (85.44% of sample 1, 84.97% of sample 3)
Pregnancies and their outcomes (miscarriage vs induced abortion) are linked from the Danish National Patient Register to the mothers, which is what defines the sample-2 and sample-3 comparison groups
Parental education length is linked from the Educational Register to the women's mothers and fathers

sample.universe: The full population of Danish mothers 1980-2014, restricted to women born 1960 to 1976 (average year of birth 1967), who are evaluated at age 40
sample.unit_of_observation: Woman ('individual observations'), nested in families ('group observations') in the sister fixed-effect samples; the event-study figures use a person-year panel from t-5 to t+16
selection_rules: Full population of Danish mothers, 1980-2014 (Statistics Denmark registers)
Exclude individuals whose datasets are incomplete in parents, number of children, age or marital status
Keep only women born from 1960 to 1976, so they can be evaluated at age 40
Classify all pregnancies as completed or aborted and distinguish miscarriages from induced abortions; exclude unspecified diagnoses
Sample 1: families in which at least one sister gave birth before turning 25 and at least one did not (34,784 families; 36,093 early and 37,042 non-early childbearing mothers)

Sample 2: women who gave birth before turning 25, plus women who did not but were pregnant before turning 25, suffered a miscarriage and did not have their first childbirth until after 25 (123,825 early and 4,880 non-early childbearing mothers); women who had an induced abortion after the miscarriage before turning 25 are excluded

Sample 3: women who gave birth before turning 25 and their non-early childbearing sisters who were pregnant before turning 25 but miscarried and did not have their first childbirth until after 25 (938 families; 1,076 early and 938 non-early childbearing mothers); sisters with an induced abortion after the miscarriage are excluded
For comparability, only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected (including women who adopt, less than 1% of total fertility)
In some families more than two sisters meet the inclusion criteria
sample.n_observations: Table 2 regressions: 73,135 (sample 1), 128,705 (sample 2) and 2,014 (sample 3) individual observations; 32,588 and 934 group observations for samples 1 and 3
sample.n_individuals: Sample 1: 36,093 early and 37,042 non-early childbearing mothers in 34,784 families; Sample 2: 123,825 early and 4,880 non-early childbearing mothers; Sample 3: 1,076 early and 938 non-early childbearing mothers in 938 families

construction_notes: All nominal variables are converted to real values using the CPI (Statistics Denmark); the tables note 1DKK≈0.13€
Yearly earnings = all labor earnings in a given year: labor income, fringe benefits, other nontaxable income, employee bonuses and realizations of stock options (IND: LOENMV)
Adult earnings = aggregated labor earnings after ages 25 to 40, the longest period the mothers could be followed; the regressions use its natural logarithm
Education length = years of education from entering elementary school to finishing the highest level of education (UDDA: HFPRIA, HFAUUD)
The health control ('Diagnoses') is the woman's average number of health diagnoses per year in adolescence (ages 12-18), excluding all diagnoses relating to pregnancy, abortion, birth and fertility
The wage rate is Statistics Denmark's estimated hourly wage (TIMELON); only high-quality observations (TLONKVAL < 40) are kept, about 70% of observations, which is why it is not a main variable
Labor participation is a dummy equal to 1 if the woman had any labor earnings in a given year

Event time t0 = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother (last miscarriage before age 25 if several); for sample 1 the early childbearing sister's age at first birth defines t0 for all sisters in the family; women are followed from t-5 to t+16
The socioeconomic heterogeneity test splits each sample at the median education length of the women's mothers (8 years); women whose mothers have exactly the median length are put in the lower group

claims.statement: Among Danish early and non-early childbearing sisters (sample 1), early childbearing (first childbirth before turning 25) significantly reduces Log(Adult Earnings).

treatment.label: Early Childbearing (EC) - first childbirth before turning 25

register_source.value: FABE (up until 1986) / BEF (thereafter): family links and personal identification numbers connecting mothers to their children; pregnancies and their outcomes from the Danish National Patient Register

definition.value: A dummy indicating early childbearing, defined as giving birth to a first child before turning 25 (first-time mothers aged 24 or younger).

timing.value: Age at first childbirth; treatment is realised before age 25 (or before the alternative cutoff age), i.e. before the ages over which the outcomes are measured

register_source.value: IND: LOENMV

definition.value: The natural logarithm of adult earnings, i.e. of aggregated labor earnings after ages 25 to 40. Yearly labor earnings are the sum of all labor income, fringe benefits, other nontaxable income, employee bonuses and realizations of stock options; nominal values are converted to real values using the CPI.

timing.value: Aggregated over ages 25 to 40; the table reports the level effect at age 40

units.value: log points of adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40

magnitude.interpretation: early childbearing before age 25 is significantly associated with lower adult earnings after ages 25 to 40, by 18.4%, in comparison to non-early childbearing sisters

estimand.target_population: Early childbearing women in families with at least one early and one non-early childbearing sister; the paper states that fixed-effects methods put most weight on women most likely to become early childbearing mothers, so the results gravitate toward the treatment effect on treated mothers
estimand.time_horizon: adult earnings aggregated after ages 25 to 40 (level effect at age 40)
estimand.formal_query: E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=1)] - E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=0)] for sample 1

population.description: Danish mothers born 1960-1976 belonging to families in which at least one sister gave birth before turning 25 and at least one did not (sample 1)
population.ages: Followed to age 40; adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40
population.selection: Sisters (women with a shared mother) in families with at least one early and one non-early childbearing sister; control women must have become mothers before turning 40; individuals with incomplete register data excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Within-family (sister) variation in the age at first childbirth: families in which at least one sister gave birth before turning 25 and at least one did not. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Strict exogeneity of family characteristics: conditional on the family (sister) fixed effect and the controls X, early childbearing is random among sisters.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the requirement and immediately calls it questionable, arguing that the problem can be partially resolved by controlling for pre-childbearing observables (health, birth order).

key_assumptions.assumption: No spillover effect in the sisters' fertility choices (no interference between sisters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for birth order but concedes these mechanisms are difficult to capture empirically; it cites Heissel (2017), who finds that teenage motherhood within the family affects sisters negatively, and notes this may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between the sisters (abilities and preferences regarding family and career) remains after the family fixed effect and may be correlated with both early childbearing and the outcome - conceded by the paper as a remaining source of bias.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; for sample 3 the paper argues the restriction of the comparison group to miscarrying sisters is what addresses this individual heterogeneity.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error is small in high-quality administrative registers, so that the within-family coefficient provides a lower bound of the coefficient of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the register nature of the data (footnote 17), citing Griliches (1979), Bound and Solon (1999) and Ribar (1999); not tested.

threats_discussed: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between sisters (ability, family and career preferences) correlated with both fertility timing and labour-market outcomes
Spillover effects in the sisters' fertility choices and differential parental investment after one sister's early birth (Heissel, 2017)
Measurement error amplified by the within-family transformation (Griliches, 1979; Bound and Solon, 1999)
Early childbearing is highly endogenous to individual features, so sisters need not be comparable
robustness_checks: Alternative age thresholds defining early childbearing: before turning 24, 23 and 22 (Tables A3-A5)

Restricting the sister samples to families with no more than three sisters (Table A8 and Fig. A7)

Event-study figure of crude means from t-5 to t+16 to inspect the common-trend assumption (Fig. 2)
Dropping the health (Diagnoses) control (untabulated; described as making the negative effect slightly smaller, with an insignificant difference)
unresolved_confounders: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between the sisters, such as abilities and preferences regarding their family and career, 'may very well bias the estimator if no further measures are taken'
Spillover effects in the sisters' fertility choices, which the paper says are difficult to fully capture empirically and may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect

claims.statement: Among Danish early childbearing women and women whose first birth was delayed by an early miscarriage (sample 2), early childbearing (first childbirth before turning 25) significantly reduces Log(Adult Earnings).

treatment.label: Early Childbearing (EC) - first childbirth before turning 25

register_source.value: FABE (up until 1986) / BEF (thereafter): family links and personal identification numbers connecting mothers to their children; pregnancies and their outcomes from the Danish National Patient Register

definition.value: A dummy indicating early childbearing, defined as giving birth to a first child before turning 25 (first-time mothers aged 24 or younger).

timing.value: Age at first childbirth; treatment is realised before age 25 (or before the alternative cutoff age), i.e. before the ages over which the outcomes are measured

register_source.value: IND: LOENMV

definition.value: The natural logarithm of adult earnings, i.e. of aggregated labor earnings after ages 25 to 40. Yearly labor earnings are the sum of all labor income, fringe benefits, other nontaxable income, employee bonuses and realizations of stock options; nominal values are converted to real values using the CPI.

timing.value: Aggregated over ages 25 to 40; the table reports the level effect at age 40

units.value: log points of adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40

magnitude.interpretation: the estimated cost of early childbearing is reduced to 9% for adult earnings

estimand.target_population: Early childbearing women compared with women who were pregnant before 25, miscarried and had their first birth only after 25; the paper states that instrumental and fixed-effects methods put most weight on women most likely to become early childbearing mothers, so the results gravitate toward the treatment effect on treated mothers
estimand.time_horizon: adult earnings aggregated after ages 25 to 40 (level effect at age 40)
estimand.formal_query: E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=1)] - E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=0)] for sample 2

population.description: Danish mothers born 1960-1976 who gave birth before turning 25, plus women who were pregnant before turning 25, suffered a miscarriage and did not have their first childbirth until after 25 (sample 2)
population.ages: Followed to age 40; adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40
population.selection: Comparison group restricted to women with an early miscarriage and no induced abortion afterwards; control women must have become mothers before turning 40; individuals with incomplete register data excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Miscarriages treated as exogenous variation in the timing of childbearing: the comparison group consists of women who were also pregnant before turning 25 but whose first childbirth was delayed by a miscarriage (and who did not have an induced abortion). Estimated by cross-sectional OLS, not by instrumental variables.

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

lhs: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25
given: Diagnoses (average number of diagnoses per year in adolescence)

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriages are biologically but not socially random: women from more disadvantaged backgrounds have a higher probability of miscarrying even after health differences are controlled for, which the paper states could bias estimates that do not address family heterogeneity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested within sample 2; the paper's answer is the sister fixed-effect estimator applied to sample 3.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

key_assumptions.assumption: The combination of the two strategies removes both biases: miscarriages provide exogenous variation in the timing of childbearing, addressing selection, while the sister fixed-effect estimator removes family and socioeconomic heterogeneity, including the social bias in miscarriages.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested directly; the paper reads the difference between the sample 1/2 and the sample 3 estimates as evidence that each strategy alone leaves bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on motherhood and on data completeness: only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected, individuals with incomplete data are excluded, and only cohorts 1960-1976 are kept; women who had an induced abortion after their early miscarriage are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2. – Time Trends, Crude Means by Sample and Early Childbearing Panel A. Yearly Earnings Panel B. Labor Participation Panel C. Marriage Panel D. Undertaking Education Note. The ﬁgures show the crude means around the event from t-5 to t+16 of the early and non-early childbearing women in Yearly Earnings (panel A), Labor Market Participation (panel B), Marital Status (panel C), and Undertaking Education (panel D). The event is deﬁned as the age of ﬁrst birth for the early childbearing mothers and as the age of miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mothers. For Sample 1, the early childbearing sister’s age at ﬁrst birth is deﬁned as the event for all sisters in the family. Labor Market Participation is a dummy taking a value of 1 if the women have any labor earnings in the given year. Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. Monetary values are converted to real values using the CPI. 1DKK≈0.13€.

register_source.value: FABE (up until 1986) / BEF (thereafter): family links and personal identification numbers connecting mothers to their children; pregnancies and their outcomes from the Danish National Patient Register

definition.value: A dummy indicating early childbearing, with early childbearing redefined as having the first childbirth before turning 22 (robustness test of the threshold age).

timing.value: Age at first childbirth; treatment is realised before age 25 (or before the alternative cutoff age), i.e. before the ages over which the outcomes are measured

register_source.value: UDDA: HFPRIA, HFAUUD

definition.value: The length of the woman's total education measured in years, from entering elementary school to finishing the highest level of education.

timing.value: Highest completed education observed at age 40

units.value: years of education

estimand.target_population: Early childbearing women in families with at least one early and one non-early childbearing sister; the paper states that fixed-effects methods put most weight on women most likely to become early childbearing mothers, so the results gravitate toward the treatment effect on treated mothers
estimand.time_horizon: education length at age 40
estimand.formal_query: E[Education (education length in years)|do(EC=1)] - E[Education (education length in years)|do(EC=0)] for sample 1

population.description: Danish mothers born 1960-1976 belonging to families in which at least one sister gave birth before turning 25 and at least one did not (sample 1)
population.ages: Followed to age 40; adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40
population.selection: Sisters (women with a shared mother) in families with at least one early and one non-early childbearing sister; control women must have become mothers before turning 40; individuals with incomplete register data excluded; early childbearing redefined as the first childbirth before turning 22

identification.source_of_variation: Within-family (sister) variation in the age at first childbirth: families in which at least one sister gave birth before turning 25 and at least one did not. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used.; early childbearing redefined as the first childbirth before turning 22

key_assumptions.assumption: Strict exogeneity of family characteristics: conditional on the family (sister) fixed effect and the controls X, early childbearing is random among sisters.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the requirement and immediately calls it questionable, arguing that the problem can be partially resolved by controlling for pre-childbearing observables (health, birth order).

rhs: Unobserved determinants of Education (education length in years)
given: Family background shared by sisters (sister fixed effect)
Diagnoses (average number of diagnoses per year in adolescence)

implies_edges.from: Family background shared by sisters (sister fixed effect)

key_assumptions.assumption: No spillover effect in the sisters' fertility choices (no interference between sisters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for birth order but concedes these mechanisms are difficult to capture empirically; it cites Heissel (2017), who finds that teenage motherhood within the family affects sisters negatively, and notes this may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between the sisters (abilities and preferences regarding family and career) remains after the family fixed effect and may be correlated with both early childbearing and the outcome - conceded by the paper as a remaining source of bias.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; for sample 3 the paper argues the restriction of the comparison group to miscarrying sisters is what addresses this individual heterogeneity.

implies_edges.from: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between sisters (ability, family and career preferences)
implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on motherhood and on data completeness: only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected, individuals with incomplete data are excluded, and only cohorts 1960-1976 are kept.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: became a mother before turning 40, complete register information, born 1960-1976

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error is small in high-quality administrative registers, so that the within-family coefficient provides a lower bound of the coefficient of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the register nature of the data (footnote 17), citing Griliches (1979), Bound and Solon (1999) and Ribar (1999); not tested.

threats_discussed: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between sisters (ability, family and career preferences) correlated with both fertility timing and labour-market outcomes
Spillover effects in the sisters' fertility choices and differential parental investment after one sister's early birth (Heissel, 2017)
Measurement error amplified by the within-family transformation (Griliches, 1979; Bound and Solon, 1999)
Early childbearing is highly endogenous to individual features, so sisters need not be comparable

Excluding sisters whose ages at first birth are more than 7 and more than 4 years apart (Table A6)

Restricting the sister samples to families with no more than three sisters (Table A8 and Fig. A7)

Event-study figure of crude means from t-5 to t+16 to inspect the common-trend assumption (Fig. 2)
Dropping the health (Diagnoses) control (untabulated; described as making the negative effect slightly smaller, with an insignificant difference)
unresolved_confounders: Unobserved individual heterogeneity between the sisters, such as abilities and preferences regarding their family and career, 'may very well bias the estimator if no further measures are taken'
Spillover effects in the sisters' fertility choices, which the paper says are difficult to fully capture empirically and may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect

claims.statement: Among Danish early childbearing women and women whose first birth was delayed by an early miscarriage (sample 2), early childbearing (first childbirth before turning 22) significantly reduces Log(Adult Earnings), early childbearing redefined as the first childbirth before turning 22.

treatment.label: Early Childbearing (EC) - first childbirth before turning 22

register_source.value: FABE (up until 1986) / BEF (thereafter): family links and personal identification numbers connecting mothers to their children; pregnancies and their outcomes from the Danish National Patient Register

definition.value: A dummy indicating early childbearing, with early childbearing redefined as having the first childbirth before turning 22 (robustness test of the threshold age).

timing.value: Age at first childbirth; treatment is realised before age 25 (or before the alternative cutoff age), i.e. before the ages over which the outcomes are measured

register_source.value: IND: LOENMV

definition.value: The natural logarithm of adult earnings, i.e. of aggregated labor earnings after ages 25 to 40. Yearly labor earnings are the sum of all labor income, fringe benefits, other nontaxable income, employee bonuses and realizations of stock options; nominal values are converted to real values using the CPI.

timing.value: Aggregated over ages 25 to 40; the table reports the level effect at age 40

units.value: log points of adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40

estimand.target_population: Early childbearing women compared with women who were pregnant before 25, miscarried and had their first birth only after 25; the paper states that instrumental and fixed-effects methods put most weight on women most likely to become early childbearing mothers, so the results gravitate toward the treatment effect on treated mothers
estimand.time_horizon: adult earnings aggregated after ages 25 to 40 (level effect at age 40)
estimand.formal_query: E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=1)] - E[Log(Adult Earnings)|do(EC=0)] for sample 2

population.description: Danish mothers born 1960-1976 who gave birth before turning 25, plus women who were pregnant before turning 25, suffered a miscarriage and did not have their first childbirth until after 25 (sample 2)
population.ages: Followed to age 40; adult earnings aggregated over ages 25 to 40
population.selection: Comparison group restricted to women with an early miscarriage and no induced abortion afterwards; control women must have become mothers before turning 40; individuals with incomplete register data excluded; early childbearing redefined as the first childbirth before turning 22

identification.source_of_variation: Miscarriages treated as exogenous variation in the timing of childbearing: the comparison group consists of women who were also pregnant before turning 25 but whose first childbirth was delayed by a miscarriage (and who did not have an induced abortion). Estimated by cross-sectional OLS, not by instrumental variables.; early childbearing redefined as the first childbirth before turning 22

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

lhs: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25
given: Diagnoses (average number of diagnoses per year in adolescence)

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

implies_edges.to: Early childbearing (EC): first childbirth before turning 25

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

lhs: Miscarriage before turning 25 (delaying first childbirth)
given: Diagnoses (average number of diagnoses per year in adolescence)

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriages are biologically but not socially random: women from more disadvantaged backgrounds have a higher probability of miscarrying even after health differences are controlled for, which the paper states could bias estimates that do not address family heterogeneity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested within sample 2; the paper's answer is the sister fixed-effect estimator applied to sample 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on motherhood and on data completeness: only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected, individuals with incomplete data are excluded, and only cohorts 1960-1976 are kept; women who had an induced abortion after their early miscarriage are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: became a mother before turning 40, complete register information, born 1960-1976; comparison women were pregnant before 25, miscarried, had no induced abortion and no first birth until after 25

threats_discussed: Miscarriages may adversely affect women psychologically, which could affect later labour-market outcomes
Women with poor health and risky behaviour during pregnancy may be more likely to miscarry, and health is correlated with labour-market outcomes; the women's behaviour cannot be observed

Miscarriages are biologically but not socially random: women from more disadvantaged backgrounds miscarry more often even after health is controlled for (Ashcraft et al., 2013; Fletcher and Wolfe, 2009)
How best to specify the health control remains an open question (all diagnoses are weighted equally)

Event-study figure of crude means from t-5 to t+16 to inspect the common-trend assumption (Fig. 2)
Dropping the health (Diagnoses) control (untabulated; described as making the negative effect slightly smaller, with an insignificant difference)

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2. – Time Trends, Crude Means by Sample and Early Childbearing Panel A. Yearly Earnings Panel B. Labor Participation Panel C. Marriage Panel D. Undertaking Education Note. The ﬁgures show the crude means around the event from t-5 to t+16 of the early and non-early childbearing women in Yearly Earnings (panel A), Labor Market Participation (panel B), Marital Status (panel C), and Undertaking Education (panel D). The event is deﬁned as the age of ﬁrst birth for the early childbearing mothers and as the age of miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mothers. For Sample 1, the early childbearing sister’s age at ﬁrst birth is deﬁned as the event for all sisters in the family. Labor Market Participation is a dummy taking a value of 1 if the women have any labor earnings in the given year. Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. Monetary values are converted to real values using the CPI. 1DKK≈0.13€.

For Sample 1, the early childbearing sister’s age at ﬁrst birth is deﬁned as the event for all sisters in the family. Labor Market Participation is a dummy taking a value of 1 if the women have any labor earnings in the given year. Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. key_assumptions.assumption: No spillover effect in the sisters' fertility choices (no interference between sisters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for birth order but concedes these mechanisms are difficult to capture empirically; it cites Heissel (2017), who finds that teenage motherhood within the family affects sisters negatively, and notes this may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect.

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

lhs: Miscarriage before turning 25 (delaying first childbirth)

key_assumptions.assumption: The combination of the two strategies removes both biases: miscarriages provide exogenous variation in the timing of childbearing, addressing selection, while the sister fixed-effect estimator removes family and socioeconomic heterogeneity, including the social bias in miscarriages.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested directly; the paper reads the difference between the sample 1/2 and the sample 3 estimates as evidence that each strategy alone leaves bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on motherhood and on data completeness: only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected, individuals with incomplete data are excluded, and only cohorts 1960-1976 are kept; women who had an induced abortion after their early miscarriage are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for birth order but concedes these mechanisms are difficult to capture empirically; it cites Heissel (2017), who finds that teenage motherhood within the family affects sisters negatively, and notes this may mean the sister fixed-effect analysis underestimates the true effect.

key_assumptions.assumption: No pre-pregnancy life-planning differences between the miscarrying and the non-miscarrying women, because all of them were pregnant at an early age with no evident intention of terminating the pregnancy; hence no correlation between early childbearing and the error term.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual evidence: the panels of Fig. 2 (event study around age at first birth / age at miscarriage) show a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance of the exogenous variation: a miscarriage before turning 25 delays the first childbirth, so the comparison women's non-early childbearing status is produced by the miscarriage rather than by a choice to postpone motherhood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction: women who had an induced abortion after the early miscarriage are excluded, so women who actively chose to postpone motherhood are removed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trend assumption: the early and the non-early childbearing women would have followed the same labour-market, education and marital trajectories in the absence of the early first birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reorganises the panel as an event study (Fig. 2, event = age at first birth for the early childbearing mother and age at miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mother) and reports a high degree of common trend before the event for samples 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Miscarriage affects later labour-market outcomes only through the delay of the first childbirth - in particular, no direct psychological effect large enough to bias the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper cites Rai & Regan (2006): severe psychological effects of miscarrying predominantly affect women with recurrent miscarriages, estimated at less than 1% of women, and concludes it is doubtful that this effect will bias the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Systematic health differences that make a woman both more likely to miscarry and worse off in the labour market are captured by the diagnoses control (average number of non-pregnancy-related diagnoses per year in adolescence).
key_assumptions.supported_by: A health control variable is included; the paper concedes that the pregnant women's behaviour cannot be observed and that concerns remain about how to specify the health variable optimally.

lhs: Miscarriage before turning 25 (delaying first childbirth)

key_assumptions.assumption: The combination of the two strategies removes both biases: miscarriages provide exogenous variation in the timing of childbearing, addressing selection, while the sister fixed-effect estimator removes family and socioeconomic heterogeneity, including the social bias in miscarriages.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested directly; the paper reads the difference between the sample 1/2 and the sample 3 estimates as evidence that each strategy alone leaves bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on motherhood and on data completeness: only control women who became mothers before turning 40 are selected, individuals with incomplete data are excluded, and only cohorts 1960-1976 are kept; women who had an induced abortion after their early miscarriage are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction; the paper discusses the resulting external-validity limitation in Section 5.1 rather than testing it.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2. – Time Trends, Crude Means by Sample and Early Childbearing Panel A. Yearly Earnings Panel B. Labor Participation Panel C. Marriage Panel D. Undertaking Education Note. The ﬁgures show the crude means around the event from t-5 to t+16 of the early and non-early childbearing women in Yearly Earnings (panel A), Labor Market Participation (panel B), Marital Status (panel C), and Undertaking Education (panel D). The event is deﬁned as the age of ﬁrst birth for the early childbearing mothers and as the age of miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mothers. For Sample 1, the early childbearing sister’s age at ﬁrst birth is deﬁned as the event for all sisters in the family. Labor Market Participation is a dummy taking a value of 1 if the women have any labor earnings in the given year. Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. Monetary values are converted to real values using the CPI. 1DKK≈0.13€.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2. – Time Trends, Crude Means by Sample and Early Childbearing Panel A. Yearly Earnings Panel B. Labor Participation Panel C. Marriage Panel D. Undertaking Education Note. The ﬁgures show the crude means around the event from t-5 to t+16 of the early and non-early childbearing women in Yearly Earnings (panel A), Labor Market Participation (panel B), Marital Status (panel C), and Undertaking Education (panel D). The event is deﬁned as the age of ﬁrst birth for the early childbearing mothers and as the age of miscarriage for the non-early childbearing mothers. For Sample 1, the early childbearing sister’s age at ﬁrst birth is deﬁned as the event for all sisters in the family. Labor Market Participation is a dummy taking a value of 1 if the women have any labor earnings in the given year. Marriage is deﬁned as either being married by law or being in a cohabiting relationship. Undertaking Education is deﬁned as not having completed their highest educational attainment. Monetary values are converted to real values using the CPI. 1DKK≈0.13€.
